present.name: Verb endings with ich, du, wir and the rest
present.about: Most verbs end in -e with ich, -st with du, -t with er, sie, es or ihr, and -en with wir, sie or Sie; if the part before -en ends in s, ß, x or z, du takes only -t: ich arbeite, du arbeitest, wir arbeiten, du heißt.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: The verb's ending says who: ich trinke, du trinkst, er trinkt, wir trinken (I drink, you drink, he drinks, we drink).

v2.name: Verb second
v2.about: In a main clause the verb comes second. Start with a time word, and the subject moves after the verb: Morgen fahren wir (tomorrow go we).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

v2.short: In a main clause the verb comes second, even after a time or a place: Hier ist mein Schlüssel (here is my key).

question.name: Questions: verb first or after the question word
question.about: In a yes-or-no question the verb comes first; after a question word, it comes next: Wo wohnst du (where live you).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: A yes-or-no question starts with the verb: Bist du fertig? (are you ready?) After a question word, the verb comes next: Wo ist das Auto?

gender.name: der, die, das
gender.about: Every noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das), and ein, kein, mein and the rest match it: der Bahnhof, die Bank, das Haus.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Every noun is a der, die or das word, and ein, mein and the rest match it: der Tisch, die Milch, das Handy.

accusative.name: den for a masculine object
accusative.about: When a masculine noun is the object of the verb, der becomes den and ein becomes einen: Ich habe den Zug verpasst (I have the train missed).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

accusative.short: A der word as the object takes den and einen: Ich habe den Schlüssel, Ich trinke einen Kaffee (I have the key, I'm having a coffee).

dative.name: dem after mit, in, auf …
dative.about: After mit, zu, von, bei, and in or auf for where something is, der and das become dem, a feminine die becomes der, and a plural die becomes den, with the noun usually adding -n: mit dem Bus (with the bus), mit den Kindern (with the children).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

dative.short: After auf, in or mit, for where something is or what it's with, der and das become dem and die becomes der: auf dem Tisch, in der Tasche.

nicht.name: Where nicht goes
nicht.about: nicht usually comes after the object and time words, near the end, but before a place word, an adjective or a verb at the end: Ich kenne ihn nicht (I know him not).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

nicht.short: nicht comes after the object, near the end, but before ready, here or home: Ich habe das Buch nicht, Ich bin nicht fertig.

kein.name: kein: no, not a
kein.about: Before a noun, German says kein (no) where English says not a or not any: Ich habe kein Auto (I have no car).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

kein.short: Before a noun, German says kein where English says not a or not any: Ich habe kein Auto (I have no car).

perfect.name: Past with haben: second verb last
perfect.about: To talk about the past with haben, put the second verb in its past form at the end: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen (I have a book read).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

perfect.short: Past with haben: the second verb, in its past form, goes to the end: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen (I have a book read).

sein-perfect.name: Past with sein
sein-perfect.about: Verbs of going from place to place, and a few more, take sein instead of haben: Wir sind nach Hamburg gefahren (we are to Hamburg traveled).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

sein-perfect.short: Verbs of going somewhere take sein instead of haben: Wir sind nach Hause gegangen (we are home gone).

modal.name: können, müssen, wollen, möchten: second verb last
modal.about: With können, müssen, wollen or möchten, the second verb goes to the end, with no word for to: Ich will heute schwimmen (I want today swim).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

modal.short: After können, müssen or wollen, the second verb goes to the end, with no word for to: Ich will Kaffee trinken (I want coffee drink).

separable.name: Separable verbs
separable.about: Verbs like aufstehen split: the verb comes second and the little word (auf) goes to the end: Ich stehe um sieben auf (I stand at seven up).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

separable.short: Verbs like aufstehen split: the verb comes second and the little word goes to the end: Ich stehe um sieben auf (I stand at seven up).

dass.name: dass: verb to the end
dass.about: After dass (that), the verb goes to the end of its clause: Ich glaube, dass sie heute arbeitet (I believe that she today works).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

dass.short: After dass (that), the verb goes to the end of its clause: Ich glaube, dass sie heute arbeitet (I believe that she today works).

weil.name: weil: because, verb last
weil.about: After weil (because), the verb goes to the end of its clause too: weil ich müde bin (because I tired am).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

weil.short: After weil (because), the verb goes to the end too: weil ich müde bin (because I tired am).

es-gibt.name: es gibt: there is
es-gibt.about: es gibt (it gives) says there is or there are, and a masculine der or ein after it becomes den or einen: Es gibt einen Park (it gives a park).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

es-gibt.short: es gibt (it gives) says there is or there are: Es gibt einen Park (there's a park).

gern.name: gern: liking to do
gern.about: To say you like doing something, put gern (gladly) after the verb: Ich trinke gern Kaffee (I drink gladly coffee).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gern.short: To say you like doing something, put gern after the verb: Ich trinke gern Kaffee (I drink gladly coffee: I like drinking coffee).

time-place.name: Time before place
time-place.about: German usually puts the time before the place: Ich fahre morgen nach München (I go tomorrow to Munich), where English often puts the time last.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

time-place.short: German puts the time before the place: Ich fahre morgen nach München (I go tomorrow to Munich).

destination.name: Going somewhere: nach, zu, in
destination.about: Use nach with cities and most countries, zu with people and places such as work, and in with places you go into: nach München, zur Arbeit, ins Kino.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

destination.short: Going somewhere: nach for cities and home (nach Hause), zu for people and work, in for places you go into: ins Kino.

possessive.name: mein, dein: my and your
possessive.about: mein (my) and dein (your, to someone you say du to) go before a der or das word, meine and deine before a die word: mein Schlüssel, mein Handy, meine Tasche. Like ein, they change with the noun's role: meinen, meinem, meiner.

source.note: Added with the German lessons, open to correction.

possessive.short: mein and dein go before a der or das word, meine and deine before a die word: mein Schlüssel, meine Tasche (my key, my bag).

demonstrative.name: dieser: this; das: that
demonstrative.about: dieser (this) matches its noun the way der, die and das do: dieser Tisch, diese Tasche, dieses Buch. On its own, das points at a thing: Das ist mein Haus (that is my house).

source.note: Added with the German lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.short: dieses goes with a das word and diese with a die word, for this: dieses Buch, diese Tasche. On its own, das is that: Das ist mein Haus.

formal-sie.name: Sie: polite you
formal-sie.about: Sie, always with a capital S, is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, to one person or more. Its verb is the same as with wir: Wissen Sie, wo das ist? (know you where that is?), Das ist für Sie (that is for you).

source.note: Added with the German lessons, open to correction.

formal-sie.short: Sie, with a capital S, is the polite you, to one person or more; its verb is the same as with wir: Wissen Sie? Wollen Sie einen Kaffee?
